comparison: Both address the mechanistic interpretation (C108-C115) that the cerebellum processes violations rather than forming expectations. OpenEval finds this interpretation well-supported by the data pattern, while the peer reviewer expresses uncertainty, questioning whether predictions and prediction errors can be separated and suggesting alternative explanations including compensation and age-related variability.

Both evaluate Experiment 2 findings (C67-C76) showing replication of VE deficits in the alphabet task. OpenEval finds the large effect size and generalization strengthen the hypothesis, while the peer reviewer affirms the experiments are 'very well thought out' and support VE deficits in cognitive tasks, providing implicit support for the replication.

Both address Experiment 3 findings (C77-C88, C113) on certainty-dependent effects. OpenEval finds the selective impairment in low similarity conditions well-supported despite acknowledging potential floor effects, while the peer reviewer affirms the study provides 'solid evidence' for the specific deficit pattern across all three experiments.

Both evaluate the synthesis of findings across experiments (C89-C92, C117). OpenEval finds the convergent evidence strongly supports domain-general VE processing, while the peer reviewer affirms this provides 'a new, invaluable data point' and makes 'a valuable contribution to the field,' explicitly noting the pattern of specific slowing with violations but not complexity.

Both address Experiment 1 findings (C56-C66). OpenEval finds the selective impairment in expectancy with appropriate statistical tests provides strong evidence, while the peer reviewer affirms the work provides 'new and solid evidence for a specific cognitive deficit' and describes the experiments as 'hypothesis-driven' and 'very well thought out.'

OpenEval evaluates Experiment 1 findings (C56-C66) as well-supported, while peer R5 questions the lack of accuracy differences (C62, C63, C72, C73), asking whether this was unexpected and how meaningful RT-only paradigms are when accuracy is matched between groups.

OpenEval finds Experiment 1 RT findings (C56-C66) well-supported with appropriate controls, while peer R6 raises concerns about motor confounds (C58), questioning whether motor dysfunction contributed to RT differences and requesting correlations with SARA scores and oculomotor function.

Both address the limitation of lacking imaging data (C103-C107). OpenEval finds the authors appropriately acknowledge this limitation while noting the value of behavioral neuropsychology, and the peer reviewer agrees, stating that while MRI would have been useful for lesion-behavior mapping, 'this does not limit the significance of the behavioural findings.'

Both evaluate participant characteristics and methodology (C37, C121-C138). OpenEval finds the use of genetically confirmed SCA6, power analysis, and demographic matching well-justified, while the peer reviewer explicitly praises testing 'a comparatively large group of patients with spinocerebellar ataxia type 6 (SCA6)' as a strength that enhances validity.

Both address main findings and conclusions (C6-C11). OpenEval finds the evidence from three experiments with convergent results supports the interpretation of selective VE impairment with appropriately hedged causal language, while the peer reviewer affirms the work provides 'new and solid evidence' showing 'specific slowing of reaction times in the presence of violations but not with task complexity.'

Both address the theoretical framework and hypothesis (C5, C43, C46, C48, C52-C55). OpenEval finds these clearly stated theoretical proposals appropriately framed as testable speculation, while the peer reviewer affirms the findings 'make a valuable contribution to the field' and provide 'a new, invaluable data point' for understanding cerebellar cognitive contributions.

Both evaluate the theoretical contribution regarding neural reuse and universal cerebellar transform (C93-C95, C116, C118-C120). OpenEval finds the convergent evidence strongly supports these theories with appropriate framing, while the peer reviewer acknowledges the valuable contribution to the field, though questions some mechanistic details about predictions versus prediction errors.

OpenEval evaluates experimental procedures (C139-C155) as clearly documented with appropriate controls including attention probes, while peer R11 requests additional information about attention probe data (C141), asking whether there were attention differences between groups or correlations with findings, expressing uncertainty about potential attention confounds.

OpenEval finds claims C1-C4, C16, C23, C26-C28 about the state of the field (cerebellar involvement in cognition accepted but mechanistic understanding incomplete) are accurate characterizations supported by citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these background/context claims.

OpenEval finds the task selection rationale (C156-C159) for using subtraction is reasonable and grounded in prior literature linking spatial procedural processes to cerebellar function. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these methodological justifications.

OpenEval finds the literature review (C12-C51) accurately characterizes mixed neuropsychological results and provides well-established theoretical background on sequential processing and VE with appropriate citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for this literature synthesis.

OpenEval finds the critique of prior theoretical proposals (C96-C102), particularly the 'continuous transformation' hypothesis, is fair and supported by citations including null findings, with the VE alternative presented as more parsimonious. No corresponding peer review evaluation found, though peer R8 touches on C102 in broader theoretical context.
